title: Exploring Students’ Multimodal Representations of Ideas About Epistemic Reading of Scientific Texts in Generative AI Tools
venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students represent their ideas about reading scientific texts generated by generative AI tools, a process the authors call GenAI-science epistemic reading. The problem addressed is that students need to draw on both their understanding of science and their understanding of GenAI in order to critically interpret AI-generated scientific information, yet existing measures in this area are often limited to Likert-scale surveys. The study asks what students’ multimodal representations of these ideas look like in terms of presentational, organisational, and orientational meanings.

The study uses a qualitative collective case study approach and develops a multimodal instrument in which students draw and write short explanations about (1) how ChatGPT/Poe generates scientific texts and (2) how they themselves read scientific texts in these tools. The authors analyze 44 students’ drawings and written responses using Lemke’s framework of presentational, organisational, and orientational meaning, and from these data they construct an analytical framework with categories such as epistemic trust, epistemic knowledge, organisational form, and representations of the nature of science and GenAI. Although the responses were collected before an explicit-reflective instructional activity that was part of a larger project, this paper focuses on the pre-instruction representations rather than testing intervention effects.

Participants were 44 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students in Hong Kong participating in extracurricular lessons. The instructional context involved a bilingual teacher who had prior online training workshops on implementing the teaching approach. Students completed the multimodal task in two classrooms before instruction, and the broader project centered on improving students’ understanding of epistemic reading of scientific texts from sources including GenAI and online media.

The main conclusion is that a multimodal approach is useful for characterising students’ ideas about GenAI-science epistemic reading in ways that standard survey instruments may miss. Students expressed a range of epistemic trust positions, including trust, critical thinking, confusion, and non-evaluation, and used different semiotic modes to express these ideas. The paper’s core contribution is an analytical framework teachers and researchers can use to diagnose and discuss students’ epistemic understanding of AI-generated scientific texts. The authors argue that such multimodal representations can serve as a richer diagnostic and instructional tool for future intervention studies on GenAI in science education.
